title: Northern Lights dazzle Greater Glasgow as aurora set to return tonight
excerpt: Eager-eyed residents across Greater Glasgow caught a glimpse of the Northern Lights as it danced across the skies of Scotland with the phenomenon set to return tonight
content:
Eager-eyed residents across Greater Glasgow caught a glimpse of the Northern Lights as it danced across the skies of Scotland with the phenomenon set to return tonight.

Stargazers were treated to a dazzling display of the Aurora Borealis as it lit up the sky over the West of Scotland on Saturday night.

Keen photographers and opportunistic residents who caught a glimpse of the event have been sharing their images of the spectacle.

See some images taken from across Glasgow and the west.

Pink skies across Loch Lomond by Rochelle. (Image: Rochelle Alexandra)

A look at Lyle Hill in Greenock by Morag Blair. (Image: Morag Blair)

Maria captured the colourful sky above Stewarton. (Image: Maria Anna)

Colours of green and purple over East Ayrshire on Saturday. (Image: JoJo Millian)

Skies above Loch Lomond by Gerry Doherty. (Image: Gerry Doherty)

The Met Office said the Northern Lights could be visible in the UK again on Sunday and Monday night.

“They could be a little weaker tonight (Sunday), so most likely seen across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England,” said forecaster Greg Dewhurst.

“They may be a little stronger again on Monday night so could be seen further south into central areas.”

The spectacle can sometimes be better seen through a camera than by the naked eye.

“Long exposure camera shots may show something each night a little further south than the above visible by eye forecast,” Mr Dewhurst added.

The phenomenon is most visible in the time around the equinoxes in spring and autumn.

It is triggered by solar activity, the Met Office said.

The sun emits charged particles known as solar wind, which, when they interact with the Earth’s magnetic field, are funnelled towards the magnetic poles.

As the energetic particles collide with gases in the upper atmosphere, they release energy as light.

Oxygen produces green and, at higher altitudes, red, while nitrogen creates blue and purple hues, the weather forecaster said.
